concepts.title: Primitive Subsistence Farming and Slash and Burn

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Primitive Subsistence Farming and Slash and Burn' refers to.
questions.a: A small-plot cultivation method that uses hand tools and household labour, where a cleared patch is burnt, cropped briefly, and abandoned once soil fertility declines so a new patch can be cleared.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Primitive Subsistence Farming and Slash and Burn'.
questions.a: Known locally as jhumming in the north-east, bewar in Madhya Pradesh, podu in Andhra Pradesh, and by other regional names; productivity stays low without fertilisers or modern inputs.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Primitive Subsistence Farming and Slash and Burn' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Types of Farming (source: jess104.txt lines 21-61)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Intensive Subsistence Farming' refers to.
questions.a: Labour-heavy cultivation on small inherited holdings in densely populated regions, where heavy doses of biochemical inputs and irrigation squeeze the maximum output from limited land.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Intensive Subsistence Farming'.
questions.a: Right of inheritance fragments holdings into uneconomical sizes, yet farmers keep raising output from the same plots because they lack other livelihoods.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Intensive Subsistence Farming' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Types of Farming (source: jess104.txt lines 69-84)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Commercial Farming and Plantation Agriculture' refers to.
questions.a: Market-oriented cultivation that uses high doses of modern inputs such as HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers and pesticides to raise productivity, with plantation as its single-crop, large-area variant linking farm and factory.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Commercial Farming and Plantation Agriculture'.
questions.a: The same crop can be commercial in one region and subsistence in another, for example rice in Haryana and Punjab versus Odisha; plantations like tea in Assam need capital, migrant labour and strong transport links.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Commercial Farming and Plantation Agriculture' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Types of Farming (source: jess104.txt lines 85-116)

concepts.title: Cropping Seasons: Rabi, Kharif and Zaid

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Cropping Seasons: Rabi, Kharif and Zaid' refers to.
questions.a: India's farm calendar divides the year into three growing seasons: a winter sown rabi season, a monsoon sown kharif season, and a short summer zaid season lying between them.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Cropping Seasons: Rabi, Kharif and Zaid'.
questions.a: Rabi crops like wheat, barley, peas, gram and mustard are harvested in summer; kharif crops like paddy, maize, jowar, bajra and cotton come with the monsoon; zaid covers watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber and fodder.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Cropping Seasons: Rabi, Kharif and Zaid' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Cropping Pattern (source: jess104.txt lines 146-189)

concepts.title: Major Food Crops: Rice, Wheat, Millets and Pulses

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Major Food Crops: Rice, Wheat, Millets and Pulses' refers to.
questions.a: India's staple cereals each need a specific temperature and rainfall band: rice demands heat above 25 degrees and over 100 cm rain, wheat needs a cool season with 50 to 75 cm rain, millets are hardy coarse grains, and pulses are protein-rich leguminous crops that fix nitrogen.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Major Food Crops: Rice, Wheat, Millets and Pulses'.
questions.a: Pulses except arhar restore soil fertility by fixing nitrogen and are grown in rotation; jowar, bajra and ragi carry high nutrition; India is the largest producer and consumer of pulses.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Major Food Crops: Rice, Wheat, Millets and Pulses' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Major Crops (source: jess104.txt lines 198-260, 333-352)

concepts.title: Beverage, Fibre and Cash Crops: Tea, Coffee, Cotton, Jute and Rubber

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Beverage, Fibre and Cash Crops: Tea, Coffee, Cotton, Jute and Rubber' refers to.
questions.a: Plantation beverages (tea and coffee) and industrial crops (cotton, jute, rubber, sugarcane, oil seeds) each carry distinct climate needs, from frost-free moist slopes for tea to equatorial humidity above 200 cm rain for rubber.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Beverage, Fibre and Cash Crops: Tea, Coffee, Cotton, Jute and Rubber'.
questions.a: Jute is the golden fibre of flood-plain soils; cotton needs 210 frost-free days on Deccan black soil; Arabica coffee from Baba Budan Hills grows in the Nilgiris; sericulture rears silkworms for silk.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Beverage, Fibre and Cash Crops: Tea, Coffee, Cotton, Jute and Rubber' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Major Crops (source: jess104.txt lines 291-314, 362-417, 487-514, 576-601)

questions.q: Calculate how many people depend on agriculture given the total population and dependence percent. Use the method 'Population Dependence on Agriculture'. Work with: dependence_percent = 5, total_population = 125000. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of farm_population.
questions.a: 6250 persons

questions.q: Find the farm dependent population for a country of given population. Use the method 'Population Dependence on Agriculture'. Work with: dependence_percent = 18, total_population = 5000. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of farm_population.
questions.a: 900 persons

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Population Dependence on Agriculture' refers to.
questions.a: Agriculture remains the livelihood backbone of the country, supporting roughly three-fifths of the people, so any estimate of the farm-dependent population scales directly with the total population and its dependence percentage.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Population Dependence on Agriculture'.
questions.a: Because about 60 per cent of people live off farming, technical and institutional reforms decide the welfare of a very large population share.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Population Dependence on Agriculture', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: farm_population = total_population * dependence_percent / 100

concepts.title: Oilseed Cropping Share of Cropped Area

questions.q: Calculate the area under oil seeds from the total cropped area. Use the method 'Oilseed Cropping Share of Cropped Area'. Work with: total_cropped_area = 500. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of oilseed_area.
questions.a: 60 sq units

questions.q: Find the cropped area covered by oilseeds given its percentage share. Use the method 'Oilseed Cropping Share of Cropped Area'. Work with: total_cropped_area = 1200. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of oilseed_area.
questions.a: 144 sq units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Oilseed Cropping Share of Cropped Area' refers to.
questions.a: Oil seeds occupy roughly one-eighth of the gross cropped area, so the land under oilseeds can be worked out directly from the total cropped area using its percentage share.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Oilseed Cropping Share of Cropped Area'.
questions.a: Different oil seeds cover about 12 per cent of the total cropped area; groundnut alone accounts for about half of the major oilseeds produced.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Oilseed Cropping Share of Cropped Area', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: oilseed_area = total_cropped_area * 12 / 100

questions.q: Calculate the share of land each landless villager receives from a bhoodan donation. Use the method 'Bhoodan Land Distribution per Villager'. Work with: donated_land = 100, landless_villagers = 1000. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of land_per_villager.
questions.a: 0.1 years

questions.q: Find the per villager land share when donated area and number of villagers are given. Use the method 'Bhoodan Land Distribution per Villager'. Work with: donated_land = 800, landless_villagers = 150. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of land_per_villager.
questions.a: 5.3333 years

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Bhoodan Land Distribution per Villager' refers to.
questions.a: In the Bhoodan movement a landowner donates a plot for the landless, and the plot is shared equally among the recipient villagers, so each villager's share equals the donated area divided by the number of landless villagers.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Bhoodan Land Distribution per Villager'.
questions.a: Vinoba Bhave's movement began at Pochampally when Shri Ram Chandra Reddy offered 80 acres for 80 landless villagers; later zamindars donated whole villages as Gramdan.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Bhoodan Land Distribution per Villager', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: land_per_villager = donated_land / landless_villagers

concepts.title: Technological and Institutional Reforms in Agriculture

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Technological and Institutional Reforms in Agriculture' refers to.
questions.a: Sustained gains in farming require institutional changes such as collectivisation, consolidation of holdings, cooperation and abolition of zamindari, plus technical support like crop insurance, Grameen banks, Kisan Credit Card and minimum support prices.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Technological and Institutional Reforms in Agriculture'.
questions.a: The Green Revolution and White Revolution (Operation Flood) raised output but concentrated gains in selected areas, prompting comprehensive land development programmes in the 1980s and 1990s.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Technological and Institutional Reforms in Agriculture' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Technological and Institutional Reforms (source: jess104.txt lines 519-625)
